templates.name: Modifier placement: past participial opener (incl. Compared with that of)
Pronoun-antecedent agreement: possessive determiner its/their vs contractions
Subject-verb agreement, relative pronoun or possessive inside subject
Plural vs possessive nouns: one- or two-slot spelling grid
Finite vs nonfinite, finite main verb
Finite vs nonfinite, to-infinitive (purpose or after “the first”)
Finite vs nonfinite, finite second or subordinate verb

items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (concession), mid-sentence blank
items.passage: Besides being constructed largely by local residents from compressed-earth bricks, ______ cooler in the Sahel’s punishing heat, since warm air escapes through a perforated clay ceiling beneath an elevated metal roof.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Burkinabè architect Diébédo Francis Kéré designed a school in Gando whose classrooms stay much
there is a school by architect Diébédo Francis Kéré in Gando, Burkina Faso, with classrooms that stay much
the school that Diébédo Francis Kéré designed for Gando, Burkina Faso, has classrooms that stay much
the air inside the classrooms of Diébédo Francis Kéré’s school in Gando, Burkina Faso, stays much
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes something constructed by local residents from compressed-earth bricks, so it must describe a building. Choice C places “the school that Diébédo Francis Kéré designed” right after the phrase, making clear that the school, not another noun, is what the residents constructed.

A.why_wrong: “Burkinabè architect Diébédo Francis Kéré” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the architect himself was constructed by local residents from bricks.

B.why_wrong: The word “there” follows the phrase, so the phrase has no noun to describe; the school appears only later, inside the clause.

D.why_wrong: “The air inside the classrooms” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the air was constructed by local residents from bricks.

items.notes: Subject: architecture (arts), Kéré's Gando primary school, built by local residents from compressed-earth bricks with a raised roof for passive cooling. Recipes W, E, N; the key is not the longest option. Run 46 words with the key, 20 words after the options; the deciding phrase (being constructed by local residents) comes before the blank and fits only a building. Review: opener changed from “Despite costing far less to construct than conventional concrete buildings”, which echoed 37e5c794 (“Despite being cheap, versatile, and easy to produce”). Every option read in the full sentence: only C gives the opener a building to describe.
band7_moves: single long run (46 words with the key) with 20 words after the options, as in 37e5c794
every option names the school, so the student must judge which noun phrase lands first, not whether the right noun appears
distractor D starts one level off the right noun (the air inside the school's classrooms)
opener (being constructed by local residents from compressed-earth bricks) that only a building can satisfy

fixes: opener “Despite costing far less to construct than conventional concrete buildings” replaced: same signal word and cost concession as the template's only band-7 official 37e5c794 (“Despite being cheap, versatile, and easy to produce”); now “Besides being constructed largely by local residents from compressed-earth bricks”, which fits only a building; options and key letter unchanged
explanation, why_wrong A and D, notes and band7_moves updated; every option re-read in the full sentence: C only

band7.why: Run length and words after the blank match 37e5c794, but each distractor fails on one visible fact (an architect, “there” or air cannot be constructed from bricks) and the right subject is the plain noun. A garden-path distractor opening with the school would need a head noun that can also be constructed (its classrooms, its roof), which makes a second answer defensible, so it stays a strong band 6.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: past participial opener describing a count (findings-type subject), passage-final blank
items.passage: Isolated trees outside forests rarely appear in coarse satellite imagery. Derived from high-resolution images that a deep-learning algorithm scanned for individual tree crowns, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: a 2020 count of the trees growing across West Africa’s drylands came to more than 1.8 billion.
the trees growing across West Africa’s drylands numbered more than 1.8 billion in a 2020 count.
researchers found more than 1.8 billion trees growing across West Africa’s drylands.
there turned out to be more than 1.8 billion trees across West Africa’s drylands.
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes something derived from satellite images, which can be a count or an estimate but not the trees themselves. Choice A places “a 2020 count of the trees” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that the count was derived from the images.

B.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W), the obvious noun one level off
B.why_wrong: “The trees” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the trees themselves were derived from satellite images.

C.why_wrong: “Researchers” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the researchers were derived from satellite images.

D.why_wrong: The word “there” follows the phrase, so the phrase has no noun to describe; the trees appear only later in the clause.

items.notes: Subject: science (ecology, remote sensing), the 2020 count of more than 1.8 billion trees in the West African Sahara, Sahel and sub-humid zone from high-resolution imagery and deep learning; no researcher named. Recipes W (the trees, keeping every fact), W (researchers), E (there). Year only in the key and the closest distractor. Key A is not the longest option. Blind solve: A.
band7_moves: right subject is a count built on the obvious noun (a 2020 count of the trees), as findings from a 2022 study in 8b017d4e and the HHI score of a less concentrated market in fced396a
hardest distractor starts with the obvious noun (the trees) and keeps every fact, including the count
passage-final full-clause options of 12 to 16 words, all grammatical on their own

fixes: option set reworded: all four carried “a 2020 count/study” and two copied 8b017d4e's distractor wording (“, according to a 2022 study” and “were found, in a 2022 study, to”); now the year sits only in the key and the closest distractor (the trees ... in a 2020 count), C is a plain agent (researchers found) and D an expletive (there turned out to be)
why_wrong C and D, notes and band7_moves updated; every option re-read in the full sentence: A only

band7.why: As in 8b017d4e and fced396a, the right subject is a count built on the obvious noun, and the closest distractor opens with that noun (the trees) and keeps every fact, so only the modifier logic separates them; options are complete, fluent clauses.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: -ing participial opener, mid-sentence blank
items.passage: In a 2005 field study in the Peruvian Amazon, biologists dislodged worker ants from branches high in the rainforest canopy to investigate whether the insects could steer their descent. Twisting in midair as they plummeted, ______ a maneuver that prevented most of them from landing on the forest floor.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the tree trunk drew the ants back toward it in a steep backward glide,
a steep backward glide toward the tree trunk was made by the ants,
the biologists watched the ants glide steeply backward toward the tree trunk,
the ants glided steeply backward toward the tree trunk,
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes creatures twisting in midair as they plummeted: the ants. Choice D places “the ants” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that the falling ants twisted in midair and glided back to the trunk.

A.why_wrong: “The tree trunk” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the trunk was twisting in midair as it plummeted.

B.recipe: passive that leaves the wrong noun as subject (V)
B.why_wrong: “A steep backward glide” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the glide was twisting in midair as it plummeted.

C.why_wrong: “The biologists” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the biologists were twisting in midair as they plummeted.

items.notes: Subject: science (animal behavior), canopy ants in the Peruvian Amazon that glide backward to the tree trunk when they fall (2005 field study); no researcher named. Band 6 (template has a band-7 official, but the plan sets 6): plain agent as the right subject; mid-sentence blank with a trailing appositive. Recipes W, V, W. Review: replaces the ants-on-stilts study, which round-1 judges named a well-known textbook study. Blind solve: D.

fixes: subject replaced: the desert-ant stilts experiment is the study round-1 judges named “a well-known textbook study” (rhetorical synthesis item 9), and the live bank had already dropped it; new subject canopy ants gliding back to the trunk (Peru, 2005; claimed in claims.txt), same template, recipes (W, V, W) and key letter
explanation, why_wrong and notes rewritten; every option re-read in the full sentence: D only

band7.why: Plain agent as the right subject (as 3.5 and 3.14) and the opener's cue (twisting in midair as they fell) sits next to the blank; the closest distractor (the biologists watched the ants ...) names the ants but leads with the wrong noun.

items.subtype: Possessive determiner: singular antecedent 16 words back, plural nouns between
items.passage: West African griots, hereditary musicians and storytellers, traditionally accompany their songs on the kora, a harp made from a large calabash gourd that is cut in half and covered with cowhide. The instrument, whose 21 strings were originally made from thin strips of antelope hide, is played upright, with ______ gourd resting against the musician’s body.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The possessive determiner refers back to “the instrument,” which is singular, and the gourd is the instrument’s. The singular possessive “its” agrees with “the instrument.”

A.why_wrong: The plural “their” does not agree with the singular “the instrument”; the plurals “strings” and “strips” sit between them but do not own the gourd.

C.why_wrong: “They’re” means “they are,” not a possessive, and it is also plural.

D.why_wrong: “It’s” means “it is” or “it has,” not the possessive “its.”

items.notes: Subject: music (arts), the kora of West African griots. Band 6: antecedent 16 words before the blank, as 2cb1ee22; plural attractors (strings, strips) inside the relative clause and griots in the first sentence; no other singular noun in the window can own a gourd. Blind solve: its.

band7.why: As 3.4 (band 6): singular antecedent 16 words back with plural nouns between (strings, strips) and a plural group (griots) a sentence back; “their” fails because the gourd belongs to the instrument and “the musician’s body” is singular.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: relative-clause verb, plural antecedent inside a singular main clause
items.passage: Dwarf mistletoes are parasitic flowering plants that extract water and nutrients from pines, spruces, and other conifers. When mature, a dwarf mistletoe’s berries, each of which contains a single sticky seed, ______ open under internal water pressure, launching the seeds as far as fifteen meters toward neighboring trees.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is “berries,” which is plural; “a dwarf mistletoe’s” and the clause “each of which contains a single sticky seed” only describe the berries. The plural verb “burst” agrees with “berries.”

B.why_wrong: The singular “bursts” does not agree with the plural subject “berries”; it matches the nearby singular words “each” and “seed,” which are not the subject.

C.why_wrong: The singular “has burst” does not agree with the plural subject “berries.”

D.why_wrong: The singular “is bursting” does not agree with the plural subject “berries.”

items.notes: Subject: science (botany), dwarf mistletoe berries bursting and flinging their seeds. Band 6 target: singular possessor before the plural head (as 863065c7 and f10b7ce4), a relative clause with its own singular verb (each of which contains), three singular attractors next to the blank, 16 run words after it. Review: replaces limpet teeth, whose frame (nanofibers that ______ it stronger) copied ee4aa2aa (structures that ______ it survive) and added record trivia (the strongest biological material). Blind solve: burst.

fixes: subject and frame replaced: “mineral nanofibers that ______ it stronger than spider silk” copied the skeleton of ee4aa2aa (“structures that ______ it survive in the deep sea”), the template's only band-6 official, and the limpet story (stronger than spider silk, the strongest biological material) is record trivia and was widely reported; new subject dwarf mistletoe seed dispersal (claimed in claims.txt), possessor-plus-plural-head frame as 863065c7 and f10b7ce4, options burst / bursts / has burst / is bursting, key letter unchanged
explanation, why_wrong and notes rewritten; every option re-read in the full sentence: burst only

band7.why: Reads at least as hard as targeted: a singular possessor before the plural head, a relative clause with its own singular verb (contains) and three singular nouns ending right at the blank, then 16 run words after it; the singular forms sound right twice, as in 1c65db8f and f10b7ce4.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: plural head behind a 25-word intervener with its own singular verb
items.passage: Parvin E’tesami (1907–1941) published only one collection of poetry during her lifetime, yet it secured her a prominent position in modern Persian literature. The disputes the poet constructs in each munazara, or debate poem, typically between a humble character and an arrogant, powerful adversary, ______ her as one of the most incisive critics of poverty and injustice in early twentieth-century Iran.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is “the disputes,” which is plural; everything from “the poet constructs” to “an arrogant, powerful adversary” describes those disputes. The plural verb “establish” agrees with “disputes.”

A.why_wrong: The singular “establishes” does not agree with the plural subject “disputes”; it matches “the poet,” the subject of the clause “the poet constructs,” and the singular nouns just before the blank.

B.why_wrong: The singular “is establishing” does not agree with the plural subject “disputes.”

D.why_wrong: The singular “has established” does not agree with the plural subject “disputes.”

items.notes: Subject: literature, the debate poems (munazarat) of Iranian poet Parvin E’tesami, whose single collection appeared in 1935. Section 6 checks: head-to-blank 19 words, five singular nouns between (poet, munazara, debate poem, character, adversary), run 38 words (30+), 16 run words after the blank (15+), intervener verb of the other number (constructs). Review: replaces Sor Juana's reply to “Sister Philothea”, the canonical figure and pseudonymous-letter frame a round-1 judge flagged. Blind solve: establish.
band7_moves: intervener is a reduced relative clause with its own singular verb, the poet constructs, as the organism uses in 1c65db8f and a person has internalized in ae439895
five singular nouns between head and blank (poet, munazara, debate poem, character, adversary)
16 words of the run after the blank; run of 38 words

fixes: subject replaced: Sor Juana's 1691 reply to “Sister Philothea” repeats the subject and frame a round-1 judge flagged (boundaries item 62: “canonical figure framed through a pseudonymous letter”), already dropped from the live bank; new subject Parvin E’tesami's debate poems (claimed in claims.txt), same band-7 settings (plural head, reduced relative with a singular verb, five singular attractors, 16 run words after the blank), same options and key letter
explanation (it also quoted “secular study”, not in the passage), why_wrong, notes and band7_moves rewritten; every option re-read in the full sentence: establish only

band7.why: Matches the band-7 R1 recipe: plural head behind five singular nouns, an intervener with its own singular verb (the poet constructs) so the wrong number sounds right twice, as in 1c65db8f and ae439895, and 16 run words after the blank.

items.subtype: Tense: past perfect, earlier-than-past cue after the blank
items.passage: Ethiopian composer Emahoy Tsegué-Maryam Guèbrou wrote solo piano compositions that combine traditional Ethiopian scales with elements of European classical music. A nun since the 1940s, she ______ in a monastery in Jerusalem for more than two decades when a 2006 compilation of her recordings finally brought her work international recognition.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The 2006 compilation is a past event, and her years in the monastery came before it and continued up to it. The past perfect “had lived” shows an action completed before another past event.

A.recipe: present simple where past perfect is needed
A.why_wrong: The present “lives” does not fit a span that ended at a past event (the 2006 compilation).

C.why_wrong: The future perfect “will have lived” points to the future, but the compilation appeared in 2006.

D.recipe: present perfect where past perfect is needed
D.why_wrong: The present perfect “has lived” describes a span that reaches the present, but this span ended at a past event: the 2006 compilation that “brought” her recognition.

items.notes: Subject: music (arts), Emahoy Tsegué-Maryam Guèbrou, in Jerusalem from 1984; the 2006 Éthiopiques compilation brought her wide attention. Plan asked band 7, but tense items stop at band 5 in CB's bank (no band-7 or band-6 R4 officials), so written as a strong band 6 per WAVE.md: the deciding cue (when ... 2006 ... brought) sits 11 to 20 words after the blank, and “for more than two decades” pulls toward the present perfect, now offered as D. No simple past offered, as in 1.24 and 1.15. Blind solve: had lived.

fixes: D “is living” (an easy reject) replaced by “has lived”, the form “for more than two decades” invites until the past “brought” arrives; still ungrammatical beside a past event, so one answer only
notes quoted “drew”, the passage says “brought”: fixed

band7.why: R4_pastperf_future has no band-7 official and CB's tense items stop at band 5, so it cannot be band 7; left a strong band 6: the deciding past verb comes 11 to 20 words after the blank and the present perfect distractor reads well until then.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular head behind a participial phrase full of plurals
items.passage: Ghanaian sculptor El Anatsui’s wall hangings ripple and shimmer like cloth. A typical hanging, assembled from thousands of flattened aluminum bottle caps joined with copper wire, ______ a different shape each time it is exhibited, since Anatsui allows curators to fold and drape his works as they choose.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject is “a typical hanging,” which is singular; the phrase “assembled from ... copper wire” only describes it. The singular verb “assumes” agrees with “hanging.”

A.why_wrong: The plural “assume” does not agree with the singular subject “hanging”; it matches the nearby plural “caps.”

B.why_wrong: The plural “are assuming” does not agree with the singular subject “hanging.”

C.why_wrong: The plural “have assumed” does not agree with the singular subject “hanging.”

items.notes: Subject: visual art, El Anatsui's bottle-cap hangings, reshaped by curators at each installation. Medium: one participial intervener with plural nouns (caps), 14 words from head to blank. Review: verb changed from take (take / are taking / have taken / takes, the option set of 2.11) to assume. Subject kept: a well-known living artist, as official items use Nick Cave, Sam Gilliam and Félix González-Torres, and no judge flagged it. Blind solve: assumes.

fixes: options were take / are taking / have taken / takes, the option set of official 2.11 word for word; verb now assume (assume / are assuming / have assumed / assumes), key letter unchanged
explanation quoted “made from”, the passage says “assembled from”: fixed
subject kept after the fame check: El Anatsui is as well known as the artists in official items (Nick Cave, Sam Gilliam, Félix González-Torres) and no round-1 judge named his fame

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive: singular possessor + plural noun, two slots
items.passage: Around 270 CE, the Kingdom of Aksum, a trading power centered in present-day northern Ethiopia, began minting its own currency in gold, silver, and bronze. The inscriptions on most of the ______ were in Greek, the language of international commerce among the merchants who frequented the Red Sea port of Adulis.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The coins belong to one kingdom, Aksum, so “kingdom’s” needs a singular possessive apostrophe. “Coins” is a plain plural (the inscriptions on most of them were in Greek), so it needs no apostrophe.

B.why_wrong: “Kingdoms” is a plain plural, but the text needs the singular possessive “kingdom’s.”

C.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
C.why_wrong: “Coin’s” is possessive, but the coins do not own anything here; the plain plural “coins” is needed.

D.why_wrong: “Kingdoms’” is a plural possessive, but the text refers to one kingdom, Aksum.

items.notes: Subject: history, Aksumite coinage from about 270 CE with Greek inscriptions. Two slots with number cues: the Kingdom of Aksum (singular possessor) and the inscriptions on most of ... (plural coins). Review: frame was “Most of the ______ (kingdom’s early coins) carried”, close to 1.16 (“many of the ______ (photographer’s early photos)”). Blind solve: kingdom’s first coins.

fixes: frame “Most of the ______ carried inscriptions” with “kingdom’s early coins” echoed official 1.16 (“many of the ______”, “photographer’s early photos”); now “The inscriptions on most of the ______ were in Greek” with “first coins”; key letter unchanged
notes quoted “bore”, the passage said “carried”: rewritten

items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (Without having ...), mid-sentence blank
items.passage: Without having taken a single botany course before age 51, ______ some 145,000 plant specimens across the Americas, including about 500 species new to science.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Mexican American botanist Ynés Mexía’s expeditions yielded
it was Mexican American botanist Ynés Mexía who gathered
the fieldwork of Mexican American botanist Ynés Mexía produced
Mexican American botanist Ynés Mexía went on to gather
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes a person who had not taken a botany class before age 51. Choice D places “Mexican American botanist Ynés Mexía” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that Mexía is the one who had not taken a class.

A.why_wrong: The subject is “expeditions,” so the sentence illogically says that Mexía’s expeditions had not taken a botany class.

B.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, so the phrase has no logical noun to describe.

C.why_wrong: The subject is “the fieldwork,” so the sentence illogically says that the fieldwork had not taken a botany class.

items.notes: Subject: science (botany), Ynés Mexía, who began studying botany at UC Berkeley at 51 and collected about 145,000 specimens. Medium: short, clear opener and a person as the right subject; recipes P, E, N; key not the shortest. Blind solve: D.

items.subtype: Tense: simple past in a relative clause, date after the blank, present-tense main clause
items.passage: Born in South Africa in 1937, writer Bessie Head was refused a passport by the country’s apartheid government. Literary critics now regard Head, who ______ the country in 1964 on an exit permit that prohibited her from ever returning, as one of Botswana’s most important novelists.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The relative clause reports a completed event dated to 1964, even though the main clause (“critics now regard”) is in the present. The simple past “left” fits an event at that past date.

A.recipe: present perfect where another tense is needed
A.why_wrong: The present perfect “has left” cannot be used with a specific past date such as 1964.

B.recipe: present simple where past is needed
B.why_wrong: The present “leaves” does not fit an event dated to 1964.

D.why_wrong: The future “will leave” does not fit an event that took place in 1964.

items.notes: Subject: literature, Bessie Head leaving South Africa on a one-way exit permit in 1964. Medium: the blank sits in a relative clause inside a present-tense main clause (critics now regard), which tempts a present or present perfect form; the date follows the blank, as the reported past in 2.12. No past perfect offered. Blind solve: left.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: relative which, singular antecedent, plural main subject
items.passage: Qanats are gently sloping tunnels that carry groundwater to the surface by gravity alone. For centuries, farmers near the Iranian city of Yazd have drawn water from the Zarch qanat, which ______ for about 70 kilometers underground.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The relative pronoun “which” refers to “the Zarch qanat,” a single tunnel. The singular verb “runs” agrees with that antecedent.

A.why_wrong: The plural “run” does not agree with the singular antecedent “the Zarch qanat”; it matches “farmers,” the subject of the main clause.

C.why_wrong: The plural “are running” does not agree with the singular antecedent “the Zarch qanat.”

D.why_wrong: The plural “have run” does not agree with the singular antecedent “the Zarch qanat.”

items.notes: Subject: history and engineering, the Zarch qanat near Yazd, about 70 km long. Medium: which takes its antecedent from the main clause, as 2.18; the main subject (farmers) and the first sentence (Qanats) are plural. Blind solve: runs.

items.subtype: Personal pronoun: object, singular antecedent
items.passage: Kusunda, an endangered language of western Nepal, has no known relationship to any other living language, including the Tibeto-Burman and Indo-Aryan languages spoken in nearby communities. Consequently, linguists classify ______ as a language isolate, as they do Basque, which is spoken in Spain and France.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pronoun refers to Kusunda, a single language that linguists classify as “a language isolate.” The singular pronoun “it” agrees with “Kusunda.”

B.why_wrong: The plural “them” does not agree with the singular “Kusunda,” and it clashes with “a language isolate.”

C.why_wrong: The plural “these” does not agree with the singular “Kusunda.”

D.why_wrong: “One” would mean some unnamed language, not Kusunda, so the sentence would not say which language is the isolate.

items.notes: Subject: social science (linguistics), Kusunda as a language isolate. Easy: the antecedent is the subject of the previous sentence; object pronoun mid-sentence, unlike the sentence-initial pronouns of b1 and b2. Blind solve: it.

items.subtype: Personal pronoun: subject of a where clause, given with its verb, plural antecedent
items.passage: Giant larvaceans, tadpole-shaped animals of the deep ocean, construct elaborate mucus filters called houses. Every day or so, the animals abandon their clogged houses and build new ones, and the discarded houses sink rapidly to the seafloor, where ______ carbon that might otherwise have remained suspended near the surface.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pronoun refers to “the discarded houses,” which is plural: the houses carry carbon down and leave it on the seafloor. The plural pronoun “they” (with its plural verb “deposit”) agrees with “houses.”

A.why_wrong: The singular “it” does not agree with the plural antecedent “houses.”

B.why_wrong: “One” is singular and indefinite, so it cannot refer back to the discarded houses.

D.why_wrong: “We” refers to the writer and reader, not to the houses that sink to the seafloor.

items.notes: Subject: science (marine biology), giant larvacean houses sinking carbon to the seafloor. Easy: the antecedent is the subject of the clause just before, with no singular noun nearby that could sink or carry carbon; pronoun given with its verb, as 1.26 and 2.4, so the verb form cannot decide. Blind solve: they deposit.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: plural head behind a participial phrase
items.passage: Nok terracotta sculptures, made in what is now central Nigeria more than two thousand years ago, ______ usually hollow, with pierced eyes and elaborately styled hair.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject is “sculptures,” which is plural; the phrase “made in ... ago” only describes them. The plural verb “are” agrees with “sculptures.”

A.why_wrong: The singular “is” does not agree with the plural subject “sculptures.”

B.why_wrong: The singular “was” does not agree with the plural subject “sculptures.”

C.why_wrong: The singular “has been” does not agree with the plural subject “sculptures.”

items.notes: Subject: visual art, Nok terracottas of central Nigeria. Easy: plural head behind a participial phrase with no opposite-number noun. Blind solve: are.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular head, no intervener
items.passage: Many flowering plants depend on wind or animals to disperse their seeds, but ice plants, succulents native primarily to southern Africa, depend on rainfall. Each seed capsule ______ only when thoroughly wet, and raindrops striking the exposed seeds then splash them away from the parent plant.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is “each seed capsule,” which is singular. The singular verb “opens” agrees with “capsule.”

A.why_wrong: The plural “open” does not agree with the singular subject “capsule.”

C.why_wrong: The plural “are opening” does not agree with the singular subject “capsule.”

D.why_wrong: The plural “have opened” does not agree with the singular subject “capsule.”

items.notes: Subject: science (plant biology), ice plants whose seed capsules open only when wet so that raindrops splash out the seeds. Easy: singular subject right before the blank, plural nouns (plants, seeds) only in the other clauses.
